root.note: Late Latin took it in as blavus, already found in Isidore of Seville. Further back, Proto-Germanic *blēwaz.

history: Many French colour words are not Latin but Germanic: bleu, blanc, blond, brun, gris. The Frankish *blāo gave Late Latin blavus and Old French blef, bloe, bleu. At first the colour was not quite blue. In the Voyage of Saint Brendan, around 1121, the word means pale, whitish or livid, the colour of a bruise. The meaning ‘the colour of the sky’ is recorded around 1150. Fittingly, un bleu is still a bruise in everyday French. English blue has a double story: Old English had blāw from the same Germanic root, but Wiktionary traces modern blue to Anglo-Norman blew, from French. So English took back, through French, a word it already had.
historyEinfach: Bleu comes from Frankish, the language of the Franks, not from Latin. In old French the word first meant ‘pale’, the colour of a sick face. A little later it meant ‘the colour of the sky’. English blue comes from French bleu. Un bleu is also the mark you get when you hit yourself.

elsewhere.text: Old English had its own word from the same root, blāw, but the modern word came in from French.
